If you flew close to the speed of light for one year, you'd come home to find your twin brother ten years older.
In 1905, a twenty six year old patent clerk named Albert Einstein made a strange claim. Light always moves at the same speed, no matter how fast you are going.
Picture light bouncing between two mirrors. On a fast rocket, it must travel a longer zig zag path, and since light cannot speed up, each tick takes longer. Time itself slows down.

Tiny particles called muons are born fifteen kilometres up in the sky, and should die after less than one kilometre. But they move so fast that their time slows, and they rain down on you every second.
In 1971, scientists flew atomic clocks around the world on passenger jets. When they landed, the clocks no longer matched the ones on the ground.
Your phone proves it too. GPS satellite clocks drift 38 millionths of a second every day. Without fixing it, your map would be off by about ten kilometres daily.
At ninety nine point five percent of light speed, one of your years equals ten on Earth. And it is the traveller who ages less, because they had to turn around and come home.
So the fastest traveller would not just leave home. They would come back to a world where everyone they loved grew old without them.
